utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, or good afternoon, even. I wonder, Mr. Theunens, if you would be so good as to take the affirmation card and read the affirmation aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not taking this witness. I want to deal with two preliminary matters if I may, and perhaps it's best if I dealt with them now, but Mr. Theunens was already in the building. Your Honour, the first deals with the expert report of General Pringle. As Your Honour knows, there is reference in that report to -- I think it's four witnesses, I give an example of Panic, Tesic, and two others. There are footnotes with his name, there are conclusions in the body of the report itself. Can I just say and repeat that which I have already said, is that we do not seek to rely upon those witnesses for the substance of the report. It really comes down to the case of the redaction of those areas, and perhaps seeking the Court's guidance in relation to it, because I don't want to come on Thursday and then find it's not agreed by all parties. What I was hoping to do was to, with a red pen, underline the passages that we do not seek to rely upon. Those are passages that are generated by the footnote of Panic or Tesic et al, and clearly by having them delineated in that way it's perfectly clear that we do not seek to rely upon them. We can redact them totally by blacking them out. I would submit that perhaps that might not be the best way and the reason is as follows: If I underline which indicates that I do not seek to rely upon it and the Court should not rely upon it, if however if Panic or Tesic gave evidence, and I was to cross-examine them, it would be, I suspect, my intention, in part at least, to try and cross-examine in part of the statement to which the expert had already referred to. Now, if for example Tesic or Panic accepted that, then the red line will be removed and it goes in as part of a conclusion process, and if it is not accepted, or Panic and Tesic do not give evidence, then they can be completely redacted. Now, I know my learned friends are worried that something may go before the Trial Chamber this week that would be considered to be prejudicial for them and that a red line is not sufficient, that the Court would not be able to clear its mind from this prejudicial material. I for my part submit that by putting a red line under that passage, the Court would be in a position to know that we do not seek to rely upon it, firstly in establishing a prima facie case, and secondly, if it becomes necessary, if those witnesses do not give evidence, it will be redacted in any event. It's a question of practice and I would seek the Court's guidance in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anyone from the Defence wish to be heard. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just because I see all of my colleagues seated, perhaps I should be the first to go. We haven't really discussed this, and I can't say that this is a joint position. First of all, good afternoon to you, Your Honours, good afternoon to all. I would like to inform the Chamber that Ivan -- Mr. Petar -- our security expert Mr. Petar Vugel [phoen] is joining the Veselin Sljivancanin Defence team today. I oppose this motion of Mr. Moore. It's not a matter of the Defence fearing that something might reach the Chamber that was said by a witness that is not favourable for any of the Defence teams. I think it's a matter of principle. This is something that you said at the beginning when you set the rules Your Honours. It's about interpreting the statement of someone, or an allegation made by someone who is not a witness in this trial. If any such persons should eventually appear as witnesses and Mr. Moore decides to confront them with their own statements in cross-examination, then one thing he can do in his final argument is to analyse and compare these witnesses' allegations with, for example, Mr. Pringle's position. By doing this, however, allegation I think we would be jumping the gun. The Chamber would have the statements and allegations available at this early stage. I don't think the Chamber would have a useful way of actually looking at these statements, but I think the approach by the OTP is definitely not in keeping with any of rules that we have agreed on. That is the first thing. And secondly, it's much too premature to say this, since we don't know whether these witnesses will be appearing or not. If these witnesses appear and now Mr. Pringle is invoking some of these allegations, so if these allegations are admitted into evidence, in some way it is only then and not before that Mr. Moore can start using and analysing these. I think this is merely a way for the OTP to tender certain statements made by certain witnesses through the back door, as it were. I think the first day when Mr. Moore moved for this it was our belief that certain corrections would be made to Mr. Pringle's expert report, and that other facts would be sought to corroborate the allegations already made. And Mr. Moore definitely said he would be informing us in the course of this week whether any changes had been made to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. First of all, good afternoon to everyone. I wish to inform you that our expert, Mr. Mile Stojkovic is joining our Defence team today. I fully support my learned friend, Mr. Lukic. There is just one thing that would I like to add, Your Honours. In a situation where my learned friend, Mr. Moore, promised to remove those parts of evidence in relation to expert reports in relation to witnesses who have not appeared before this Chamber, the Defence believes there will be no need to cross-examine the expert on those topics. Should we be facing a situation where my colleague Mr. Moore decided to additionally tender evidence that the witness was not cross-examined on, I think that would be a procedural exception to this case. As for everything else, I am fully in agreement with Mr. Lukic. If Mr. Moore wishes to underline a finding, he might as well want to do it in black. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. We have with us today Mr. Bozidar Forcan, our expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber welcomes the three Defence expert witnesses. In respect of the motion, Mr. Moore, it should not be overlooked that when this matter was debated earlier, the Chamber indicated what is the normal position with an expert report. Which is that the report itself is a document, which should be before the Chamber. If, in that report, reliance is based upon certain factual and other material which is not agreed and which is not proved, then that part of the report loses its value, loses its persuasive strength. That being the view of the Chamber, a red underlining is both a wise precaution and an adequate measure to identify those parts of the report of Mr. Theunens which would, on the -- Pringle on the anticipation of the Prosecution is not going to be proved by other evidence led by the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber is entirely capable of putting out of its mind the three -- the underlined red parts. We've had to put out of our mind already quite a substantial body, the red lining cautions us and will constantly remind us as we turn to the report, which parts have not been established by evidence. That course will not require that the Defence cross-examine on the red underlined parts. Should it later occur that any of those red underlined parts comes to be established, then an issue of whether there is need to recall to cross-examine will arise. But we don't need to spend time cross-examining against the possibility that something unknown in the future may occur. Now, is that clear enough, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for that guidance. There are two other matters. The first -- I am aware of time constraints, but it does assist. The second relates to what I call bar-table exhibits. It is the Prosecution's intention to adduce from the bar table, in part, and I give one example. The indictment that, whilst used for the trial in Belgrade for the individuals who were charged with the killing at Ovcara, we would seek to put that in. And secondly, the findings of guilt in relation to the individuals concerned. Not the sentence in any way at all. We would submit that that is highly relevant evidence, and I do not know if my learned friends have any position in respect of that. I would hope not. It is a judicial finding as a consequence of the trial. I only require names and whether in actual fact there are findings in relation to the individuals concerned. In the indictment the Court will of course remember certain aspects of the particulars themselves, namely, and I use the English terminology here, if I may, the co-conspirators Vujanovic and Vujic, who were in charge of the Leva Supoderica, Petrova Gora et al., and therefore they were on trial at Belgrade, they were found guilty in relation to the killings at that time, and we would seek to establish that evidence under, I think it's under 89(C) as being relevant evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This Court -- this Chamber has constantly received, as it's been tendered, evidence of judicial proceedings by the written record, so that that would appear to be the course to be followed here. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have the written record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I might be a little late. But please allow me to give you a joint position of all our Defence teams. If my learned friend wishes to tender into evidence a sentence that has not yet taken effect, I don't think that would be a justified move. In that sentence there might be elements aggravating the position of the accused here. But unless the Chamber has everything that is in that sentence, and if everything that is in that sentence is based on defence by remaining silent, which some of the accused did, and as accused they even had the right to lie - they tried to shift the blame to the JNA - then this is a state of facts I find we can hardly discuss here. Especially since this is not a final ruling by the court, not a final sentence. There is no one we can consult in relation to this document or to this sentence that is simply not final. Regardless of everything they have been showing witnesses here we could have had someone who check about this document with, but things being what they are, I don't think that a sentence that is not final should be used in these proceedings. That would be highly prejudicial to the accused in this trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, may I ask, in what sense do you say the sentence is not final? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, under the Law on Criminal Procedure the accused have lodged an appeal. The Supreme Court of Serbia might, for example, overturn that statement. We could tender that into evidence here, but there is no evidence because the sentence is just not there, it is not final, it has not yet been ratified or confirmed by is a higher-level court, by the Supreme Court of Serbia. The destiny of this ruling of this sentence is still unknown, in other words. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just indicate, I do not wish to put the sentence in, and I did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you're reading "sentence" in an English sense, rather than the sense intended by Mr. Borovic, which I think is the judgement. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're all mindful of the time, Your Honours. According to our Law on Criminal Procedure, an appeal starts when a written motion is submitted. According to what I know right now, the judgement was drafted these very days and the appeals have not yet been submitted. It's still within the dead-line, as it were. This is the status of the Belgrade trial as we speak. A draft of the first instance judgement has been produced right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the view of the Chamber the written record of the court is admissable. What weight can attach to it is affected by the fact that there may be an appeal. By the time we come to consider it, it will be clear whether there is an appeal, and it may be that the appeal has been disposed of, it may be that it is still pending. And we will then have to accord weight to it according to those circumstances. So it will be received, Mr. Moore, but it's in a somewhat contingent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, there is a third point. And we did mention it on Thursday. Ms. Regue would like to seek the Court's indulgence to argue the points on the agreed facts. We have come a long way in time, but there are certain agreed facts that really we must get to grips with if we are to conclude this case. And perhaps that matter can be clarified and then the matter is finished. And we would seek judicial assistance in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I would like to deal briefly with two issues regarding two agreed facts, I will be very brief to we can start with the next witness. First I would like to address my learned friend's submission last week regarding this matter, because they presented to the Trial Chamber an account of facts which actually doesn't correspond with what we have been experiencing for the last two months. My learned friends were putting to the Trial Chamber why nothing have been filed actually, and the answer is very simple, is because we didn't receive a response from their side, a complete response regarding your clarifications until last week. By mid-April the Trial Chamber requested clarification concerning eight facts. We submitted to the Defence a memorandum, the 27th of April. We also -- we supported our positions with evidence. They respond to us the 10th of May. They agreed to some of these facts and they disagree with other. But they didn't provide with any -- they provide with some alternative dates, but they didn't provide with any supporting evidence that we could rely upon. They literally ended their e-mail with "we do accept suggested versions," and we took that as it sounds. And we submitted to them two more proposals, one by mid-May and another one like 10 days ago. We were informed they were quite busy and it was very difficult for them to get together and to get a common position. We understand that there is quite a lot of work to do, but this cannot be used now against the Prosecution why we have not filed any motion. There was a common understanding that we will file something once the eight facts will be clarified in a positive or in a negative way. And then we will file an addendum or we will file an amended version to the original motion. Also, this next point, the Defence also put it to the Trial Chamber that the -- out of these eight facts in the original mail of the 10th of May, we agreed to some of these facts. And now we are trying to modify two of these facts. This statement is not accurate. Just -- I don't want to go into the tales, to details, but just to give you an example we just trying to correct a grammatical point, and we informed my learned friends informally about that by mid-May and they didn't seem to have any problem but they put that the Trial Chamber last week. And when we were not aware of that submission, we actually informed to them that we didn't have any problem to go back to the other word, because it was a simple word that we changed. Just to cut this story short, Your Honours, it is the Prosecution's submission that we have been trying since the very beginning to provide to our learned friends with one -- with versions with actually -- with a proposition which could be agreeable by both parties, but it still could leave some of the conflicted points to be proved in trial. And also we could provide also to the Trial Chamber some sort of understanding. It was -- a good example was the one that Mr. Moore actually gave last week. We have also been providing some evidence that our learned friends could rely upon and that has been not the case from the Defence. And also we actually have been encounter quite difficulties because we have received of their response on the 10th of May and the second time that they have been given us some sort of feedback has been actually last week. And, well, Your Honours, the best solution that at this point we can provide to you is to file an addendum with the facts that we have agreed, and then to leave the not agreed points to be proved in court by the expert witness. And that's the first issue that I would like to deal in respect to the submission that my learned friends made last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So there are a number of matters that have been agreed and you are in a position to file now a memorandum of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: But we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are some matters that the not yet agreed and you propose, therefore, to deal with those in the course of the expert evidence this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, when can we have the written record of the agreed facts?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Well, we provide -- we will provide actually the draft to the -- to our learned friends this afternoon, if a sign or two can be reached this afternoon or early morning tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the sooner the better, because the evidence will be proceeding this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And the second point that actually I would like to deal, is fact 26, which actually is one fact which is not within the facts that Your Honours were asking clarification. Actually, this fact deals with the blockade of the barracks in the [indiscernible] operation. This will – as it reads, these facts -- this fact is in the course of the spring and summer of 1991 blockades of JNA barracks by Croatian forces began in the territory of Croatia. That fact was actually included in the motion of the 16th of March of this year. Upon revision and reflection of our material, we have 65 ter evidence that shows that the blockades started as of summer. We have informed this issue to our learned friends in May, but we didn't receive a response until last week and actually they don't agree to modify this point. And actually, this material is contained in the report of the next witness, Mr. Reynaud Theunens. So as an agreement has not been reached, we would like to remove this fact from the original motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you want leave to withdraw that as a proposed agreed fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, you have leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We look forward to the papers on what is actually agreed being filed as soon as possible. I think it really should be by tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic. I hadn't turned to any Defence counsel, because it seemed to me that this was not a matter about which there needed to be any debate. You -- there, we are told, has been agreement reached on certain facts. The Chamber is concerned to know what those facts are. It's not concerned what hasn't been agreed because that will have to be proved by the Prosecution. And for that reason we have not taken any particular notice of the course of debate between parties. We just want to know what the end product is, and that will be received in a document signed by counsel for all parties. That being so, it didn't seem to us we needed to spend time this morning hearing an explanation as to what has or has not gone on. Now, with that in your ears, is there anything further you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I fully understand this instruction. We need to be very brief. I spoke about the agreed facts some days ago. The only thing I would like it say in addition is that we approached the OTP very openly, saying that the agreed facts outside those eight that have been tabled again for discussion will not be challenged. However, we have received an offer, we're not talking about 26 facts now, we're talking about more. The OTP are therefore challenging our entire agreement on agreed facts, as it were. One which was filed and submitted to the Chamber some time ago. We shall be submitting a motion on this to the Trial Chamber anyway. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the position is clear then. Thank you, Ms. Regue. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you state your name, please?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: My name is Reynaud Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us where you live?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: At the moment I live in two places. I live in The Hague and I live in Belgium, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. And where do you work?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I work in the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY, and more specifically in a department known as the military analysis team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Have you ever testified before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia as a -- as an expert on military experts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I testified in January, February 2004 in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic, and then in January, February 2006 I testified in the trial of Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown 0600-5684. ERN 0600-5684. Do you have that two-page document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an overview of my curriculum vitae for court purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, could we move to ERN number 0461-9882.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Which is your report, sir.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You have it in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, just for a matter of background, that is a two-part report. The first part is titled, "Structure, command and control and discipline of the SFRY armed forces." And the second section is titled "SFRY armed forces OG South and the operations in SBWS"; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is correct, and the SBWS stands for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, i.e., Eastern Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'd like to offer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will receive first the curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 577, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, I see Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one procedural question that we have to deal with before we start with this in relation to the report. Mr. Weiner tells us that he wishes to tender about 150 documents with the report. We do have objections to raise in relation to some of the documents. This has nothing to do with the report as such. But Mr. Weiner said he would be raising the issue and tendering these at the end. It is at the outset that I wish to inform the Chamber if indeed the OTP decide to do that at the end, we do have objections to raise in connection with some of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. These are documents additional to the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I believe he's referring to the documents that were footnoted in the report, that the report refers to in the footnotes. We filed a motion last week --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, yes. The report itself then will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 578, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally may the witness be shown 0600-8203, which is a corrigendum. 0600-8203.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that your corrigendum, sir? Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I have a hard copy in front of me, but it's not visible on the monitor yet, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is it visible now, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Not on mine. I have the B/C/S version of my report, but for me it's fine. I have hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber has hard copies if that's going to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you file a corrigendum, did you prepare a corrigendum?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. Last week a corrigendum was prepared to correct certain errors or typographical errors in footnotes as well as typographical errors in the content of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the hard copy is five pages in English and five pages in -- three pages in English and five pages in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The English is three pages, I don't have the B/C/S in front of me, but I would assume it's more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We would like to offer 0600-8203, the three-page corrigendum, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Together with the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which is finishing 8205. They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 579, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to discuss a few concepts with you, which you mentioned in your paper, just briefly. First, command and control, what is it, why is it important?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the issue or the theoretical background of command and control as it applied to the SFRY armed forces consisting of JNA and TO is explained in the first part of the report. More specifically, in the sections 3 and 4 whereby for the purposes of this report, section 4 is the most important. In that section I provide an overview of the definitions that are given in JNA or SFRY armed forces regulations and manuals pertaining to command and control. In the English version on page 38 you can find an excerpt of the 1990 rule corps of ground forces regulation which has already been exhibited in this trial under Exhibit Number 398. And the definition has been taken from paragraph 63 of that regulation. On the next page there is a discussion of the definition as it is provided in Exhibit 395, which is the 1984 -- which are the 1984 JNA brigade rules applying to infantry, motorised, mechanised and mountainous brigades. And that comes from paragraph 107 in that regulation. I don't know whether I have to read out the regulation, but the most important in that context are the functions of command and control because they explain of what command and control consists, five functions: Planning, organisation, command, coordination, and control. And they are explained on the pages 41 to 43 of the report, whereby the content is based on Exhibit 398, paragraphs 110, if I'm not wrong, until 112.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, why is it -- why is it important, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Command and control is actually -- is a basic aspect of the functioning of armies, and I think the easiest is to look at functions of command and control, which I mentioned start on page on 41. And more specifically the function of command. Command basically consists of the assigning of tasks to subordinates. And that's the basic principles, one of the basic principles of how armies function.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, is this applicable to all units?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it is not only applicable to all units, starting from the lowest level, the squad, which is an infantry, approximately 10 people, to the highest level, the army level, but it also applies to most armies I'm familiar with. I mean, when I compare what I read and studied in JNA regulations with what I've seen in my own -- or the army in which I serve, i.e. the Belgian armed forces, these functions and then also the principles are exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do these principles apply to operational groups or operations groups?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. There is a definition for operational groups and other ad hoc formations further on in the report, but the fact that operational groups or assault detachments or assault groups are ad hoc formations and that they are only established for a specific operation in a specific area during a specific time period does not change the concept of command and control, including its functions and -- and its three principles, which are single authority, unity of command, and the obligation to implement decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you explain single authority and unity of command?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are two of the three principles of command and control, which can be found in Article 112 of the 1982 All People's Defence law. And that's Exhibit 392. It's explained in my report, pages 43 to 44. Basically, single authority means in simple terms that there is only one commander who can issue orders and to whom the implementation of these orders is reported to. Unity of command has to do with defence doctrine. It means that there is a single concept in the defence, as I found in regulations, in the defence of the country, but in simple terms it means that there needs to be coherence between the orders from the highest command level, i.e. the Supreme Command, and the instructions or the orders received by the lowest level in the chain of command and that would be the squadron leader -- the squad leader, excuse me, so the subunit of a platoon, i.e. there needs to be coherence and one view or unity in these orders throughout the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you talk about the duties of a commander. Would you please turn to Exhibit 394, page 28, please? May the witness be shown that document? In the middle that document it says, "He," referring to the commander "cannot delegate the responsibility for the situation in the unit and its use." Why can't a commander delegate responsibility?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, the commander as regulations say, can delegate some of his powers, but he cannot delegate his responsibility. This is just based on -- I mean, it's inherent to command and control, i.e. that the commander, because of these three principles, single authority, unity of command and obligation to implement decisions, is responsible. You cannot issue orders without being responsible for the implementation of these orders, and that is visible throughout not only SFRY armed forces regulations I studied for this report, but also it is applicable to other armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, could you look at another document, which is 65 ter 968. 65 ter 968, which is "Regulations on the Responsibility of the Land Army Corps' Command in Peacetime." Could you look at Article 6, which is page 4, which is tab 2 in the notebook supplied to the Court. Is this document related, or is Article 6 of this document related or similar to Exhibit 394, which you've just seen?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I have the B/C/S version in front of me, but I looked at this regulation when putting together this report. Indeed it mentions the same, so that the commander in this particular case, the corps commander can delegate some of his powers, for example the power to command or the power to control, I mean by this that these powers refer to the function of command and control, but he will still remain responsible or he will continue to bear responsibility for the situation in his units and for the work of the officers to whom he transferred some of his right -- rights. And I can explain that these officer, these can be officers from the command, i.e. officers from the staff, and then within -- outside the staff, but still part of the command are other officers who are directly subordinate to the commander instead of members of the staff who are subordinated to the Chief of Staff, but the commander, for example the brigade commander can also delegate certain powers to his battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this document says that these regulations apply in peacetime. Would these documents -- I'm sorry, would these principles or regulations also apply in wartime?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on the regulations I reviewed to compile part 1 of the report, I first looked at general regulations that define command and control in the SFRY armed forces which means they are applicable to all units where command and control units and institutions actually where command and control is being applied. I also looked at battalion, infantry battalion regulations, infantry brigade regulations and corps regulations and obviously because of the principle of unity of command, all these regulations are coherence on this and other aspects of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So would this principle or doctrine also apply with regard to an operation group?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, they apply to all units, and in all circumstances unless it is specified differently, but I haven't found such a different specification, so both wartime, emergency situation, even in threat of war in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would like to offer that document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 580, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's continue speaking about operational groups. Who was in charge or who has overall responsibility for an operations group?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Like in -- in Your Honours, like in any military unit or institution, it is the commander who is in charge and will therefore be responsible for the situation in his unit, including the subordinate units and the way how the assignments he has received are implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What are some of the different subordinate units, the various units within an operations group?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, operational groups, tactical groups assault detachments and assault groups are discussed, English version, page 96 until page 99 in the first part of my report. According to SFRY armed forces documentation as well as orders that apply to the use of SFRY armed forces the in conflict in Croatia during the latter half of 1991, an operational group can consist of tactical groups that was -- I've seen examples of tactical groups in the western part of Croatia. Assault detachments, so instead of tactical groups there can be assault detachments, and assault detachments can consist of assault groups. But I have also seen examples where an operational group just consists of battalions, elements of a brigade. So it's really up to the commander of the operational group to organise his forces in the best way that allows to carry out the assignment he has received from his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the commander has -- is in charge. Who else has command powers?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, based on what we discussed earlier about the option or the possibility for the commander to delegate some of his powers, anybody to whom the commander delegates powers, i.e. functions of command and control, the authority to command or to control or to plan or to organise or to coordinate can have, in such circumstances, a command powers. And -- or it can have these powers. And obviously because of how units the corps commander cannot issue orders to the last soldier, so there is a chain of command through which orders are being issued, i.e. there is an instruction or a directive of the Supreme Command, so the civilian leadership, if I can call it like that. And this is then through the chain of command transformed into orders or commands for the soldiers to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to those persons who the commander authorises or assigned certain duties to, that then has command and control powers, who else? What about the people in the units, who would have responsibility?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should have been more clear, I think, in my previous answer, but it's basically the subordinate units of the unit and in this case an operational group, they will have command responsibility or they will have -- or command powers for their unit. However, again, based on my review of -- of SFRY armed forces regulations, if an operational group, for example, consists of, let's say, four assault detachments, it doesn't mean that the operational group commander can delegate his responsibility to the four assault detachment commanders and that the assault detachment commanders have the full responsibility for this happening in their zone. The doctrine is quite clear, that is that in such a situation assault detachment commands will have a responsibility, but the commander, i.e. the operational group commander will still maintain the overall responsibility for what is happening in the zone of responsibility of the operational group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said the -- you indicated that the commanders of subordinate units have command responsibility. Would a commander of an assault group or a company be able to issue orders?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, like I mentioned earlier, and it's all based on review of SFRY armed forces doctrine, there are no limitations on command. If you look at the various regulations from the company level to the highest level, you will always find when the responsibilities or the duties of the commander are discussed, that the commander issues orders or that the commander, whatever command level or unit level is responsible for the implementation of the received assignments. Now, you can only ensure the implementation of an assignment that has been received by issuing as it is called in doctrine by issuing other assignments which is done on the company level by orders or commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's move to military operations. Who can be placed in charge of a military operation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, basically every person who -- the person who issues the assignment to carry out the military operation can be put in charge of such an operation. Now, this is a very theoretical answer. In practice it has to be somebody, most often an officer when we talk about an operation, who is in a position to -- who -- I apologise, in the views of the commander who issues the assignment to carry out the operation is in a position to carry out that assignment in a successful way. So the most obvious offices to do so are the commanders of the units that have been tasked to carry out the assignment, but the commander, based again on this possibility to delegate certain of his powers can also appoint any other officer from the command, from the staff, or any officer he considers to be capable of carrying out the assignment in a successful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can a commander of an operational group assign another officer to be in charge of military operations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, this follows from what I mentioned from my reply earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the officer who is placed in charge of a military operation, will he have the powers to issue orders?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the powers of that officer will be determined by the assignment he has received from his commander. It is the commander who decides which powers this officer to whom he delegated certain powers will have. If -- you mentioned that he will be placed in charge of a military operation, well, to be placed in charge implies that one is able to issue orders, i.e. that the person was received -- this delegation has command powers. It should also imply control powers, i.e. that the officer who has been -- to whom these powers have been delegated to can verify the degree of implementation of these orders and take corrective action. Again, I always refer to the functions of command and control as they have been defined in the JNA regulations. The officers to whom these powers have been delegated to can also have powers to coordinate or to plan or to organise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, speaking of planning, is planning a function of command and control?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. It's actually a very important function of command and control. In the report there is an entire section on the planning and conduct of what is called combat operations, and that's on section 6, which covers the pages 100 to 120 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is planning involved in all military operations, some specified military operations, many, a few?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Planning doesn't only apply to all military operations, but according to the JNA military lexicon, and I have not included this definition in my record, but an operation is actually the highest form of -- of -- well, combat operation is the highest form of combat activity, and action or akcija is the lowest form, for all forms of -- call it military activity, there will be a degree of planning according to common procedures which have been determined for these various types of military activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit 395, section 126, and page 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to use this opportunity. We could get DHS on our screens for the benefit of our clients.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is there a technical problem, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is a technical problem. You're wanting it on the screen in English; the Defence wants it on the screen in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I have a copy in front of me, the witness has a copy in front of him. We could use B/C/S on the screen, and Your Honours also have a copy. So we could refer to the various superior sections and assist the defendants in their language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in this discussion of planning they talk about monitoring, constant monitoring. What is the reason for constant monitoring?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, constant monitoring has to do with something that is called in military slang, situational awareness. The commander and those involved in the planning have to know what the situation is and how the situation can develop in order to prepare a plan which is able -- which can be implemented and which is also the best possible reflection or -- I will correct it, the best -- which offers the best possible preparation to continue then with the other steps of the preparation of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, there is also a reference to, in planning, to predicting events and forecasting. What is involved in forecasting and predicting events?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Forecasting or predicting events is something that I found in, among other things but in Exhibit 394. Which is the 1983 JNA text-book on command and control. It means, or it implies that the commander and those involved in preparing a combat operations within reasonable limits, based on their monitoring of the situation, have to be able to analyse and predict possible developments of the situation, covering all aspects that are considered relevant for the planning. What I mean by this is that, for example, when the commander has received an assignment to carry out an attack, let's call it an infantry attack, he and his staff will have to know not only what the enemy in front of them is -- let's call it in front of them is doing, but how the enemy can react or what the enemy can do. They will also have to know how the weather can develop. An attack in dry weather can be significantly different from an attack in foggy weather, for example, with poor visibility. They will also have to know for example or be able to predict the status of materiel, of their equipment. It could be that some equipment is in poor condition and will affect -- or that some equipment will not be repaired and this will also affect the capabilities of their own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, is the status or the attitudes, the activities of the local population, is that a factor for analysis, as part of the prediction process of forecasting?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. If the -- the situation is as such that there is still local population, and also is -- the assignment that has been received -- I will rephrase that. If the local population can have an influence, whatever influence that may be on the assignment, and how this assignment will be carried out, then obviously the attitude of the local population is one of the factors that has to be taken into account for the planning. And to answer the question, it's not only the attitude as it is now, but also the possible reaction of the population on the assignment that has been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, as part of forecasting, in Exhibit 394 at page 38 it says, "A commander or staff must be able to see in advance if the situation will change in way, and what likely course the forthcoming combat operation may take." The question, sir, is, does that place an obligation on a commander to predict events or forecast, as part of planning?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is this obligation applicable to all military operations, or all military activities?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. And of course it's most obvious with combat operations but it applies to all forms of military activity and all levels of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you are making your predictions would you -- I assume you consider various factors, but is the discipline of one's troops, is that a factor for consideration?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. As I mentioned earlier, the commander has to take into account all factors that can have an influence on the implementation of the task, because his task is to -- or his task is to implement the assignment he has received from his superior in a successful manner. So obviously if for example among his units there are units that are less disciplined or maybe there are subunits that have a problem with discipline, then he may be careful to use these units and if he has other units available, he will use these other units, for example. These are just examples, huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In obtaining information for an operation or for any activity, you have discussed in your report on page 79, you discuss the doctrine of two levels down. What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, page 60 of your report.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The reference to the two levels down comes from Exhibit 393. More specifically, paragraph 358 in this exhibit, which is -- which are the -- which is the 1983 JNA manual for the work of commands and staffs. The heading for this paragraph says -- talks about duties -- if I recall well, duties for the commander in -- during an attack. But actually from my work here, and I mean by that conversations during witness interviews, interviews of senior JNA officers for this case, as well as other cases, it is clear that this obligation applies to all military scenarios. And as it says in this paragraph, 358, the command, i.e. the staff, has to be able to provide the commander at any time during combat with detailed information about the activity and intentions of the enemy. The status activities, capabilities, and decisions of the subordinate units and to submit proposals for decision. Then the paragraph continues stating, "A commander must, at all times, know the status, position and capabilities of his units two levels down." In practical terms it means that a brigade commander has to know the situation of his companies because otherwise the brigade commander cannot issue orders to his battalions. Because it -- it -- in the battalions it will be the companies that will carry out the assignment. Now, if one of the battalions has suffered significant losses and has less forces, less companies available, this will obviously have an impact for the capabilities of that battalion. So therefore, in order to give orders or assignments to battalion, the commander, the brigade has to know how the companies in that battalion are doing. And the same would apply to an operational group and its subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to page 79 in your report, speaking of operational groups? And please tell us -- you have a diagram of Operational Group South. Could you tell us what two levels down is from the commander?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Is this in the second part of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Second part of the report, yes. Page 79.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a graphic representation of Exhibit 410, which was the -- or which is the OG South order number 235-1. I've only put the main units on this diagram, i.e. the combat units, including the staff of the operational group. Some of the information, some of the names originate from other sources but any way, to answer the question, we have the operational group and the first level below the operational group are assault detachments. Two of the assault detachments have been specified here, the 1st Assault Detachment and the second one. And because the brigade order or the OG South order does not specify the detailed organisation of the assault detachment, I've only been able to list forces that are included in this assault detachment and this overview with 1st motorised battalion, the 1st and 2nd company of the military police battalion, Leva Supoderica, Petrova Gora, and other units, this comes from the order 235-1, which is Exhibit 410. Now, depending on how the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment has organised his units, the commander of the operational group will have to be familiar with the capabilities and the situation within the subordinate units of the assault detachment in order to be able to give assignments or issue orders to that assault detachment because if the commander of the operational group does not know the situation within the assault detachment, i.e. the situation of the subordinate units, he cannot give orders to carry out certain activities or operations to the assault detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we're still discussing planning, let's move to the planning of an evacuation operation. Is planning involved in an evacuation operation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Because of the definition of an operation, whatever nature the operation has, there will be a planning phase in order to prepare as one of the aspects to prepare such an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just generally, what type of factors are considered?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would say first of all it depends of the type of evacuation. There can be evacuations whereby, for example, hostages have to be liberated somewhere and evacuated. It could be that population has -- the civil population has to be evacuated because of natural disaster. It could be that prisoners have to be evacuated, it -- I don't know which -- which type of evacuation operation you specifically want to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Take one involving prisoners.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: If -- an evacuation operation of prisoners implies that prisoners have to be moved from one location to another location. It's clear from -- I mean at first glance, that first of all one doesn't want prisoners to -- to escape, and on the other hand the aim is to arrive at the same number of prisoners at the end stage as the number that was present at the beginning of the evacuation. In practical terms a lot of factors have to be taken into account. The prisoners have to be collected at the first location, so the location from where they have to be evacuated. They have to be escorted via a certain route, and then they have to be delivered at another location. So all possible factors that can play a role, I mean it's a very general answer, but otherwise I think it's going to be very detailed, will have to be taken into account when the operation is being planned. But I think most obviously in this context is -- would be the nature of the prisoners, their medical condition or other aspects that -- that influence their condition, their situation in the -- in the area through which they have to be escorted, conditions of the road, any risk of -- of ambushes, risk of interference of other people. I -- to liberate certain prisoners or to prevent the prisoners from -- from being evacuated. Circumstances -- excuse me, the distance over which they have to be evacuated and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, as part of the planning for an evacuation and you just mentioned the various aspects, is security one of the aspects for consideration?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, security organs and their duties are being discussed in the first part of my report, page 76 to page 82. Coming back to the question, obviously the security organs, due to the official tasks, are the best placed to prepare a security assessment. So they will assist in the plan, they will participate in the planning phase to study, analyse, and then provide advice to the commander of the evacuation operation in relation to possible security risks that can interfere with the evacuation. For example, the threat of ambushes, the threat of the risk, I mean risk of -- of people friendly to the prisoners to liberate them. On the opposite side, if the local population or local armed forces consist risk then the security organs will also have to provide an assessment on that level. And the security organs, as we know from the regulations that apply to the security organs, also advise the commander as the -- for the use of the military police, will obviously play an important role in an evacuation operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In an evacuation operation, is someone usually in charge?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, it's like any operation. There needs to be somebody in charge in order to carry out the functions of command and control, and ensure a smooth execution or implementation of the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If this -- if we're dealing an operational group, who appoints that person in charge of these -- of an evacuation operation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It would be the commander of the operational group, Your Honours, unless specified differently. But then if it's done by somebody else, then it has to be done in consultation with the operational group commander or at least he has to be notified.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And once a person was named the commander of an evacuation, what powers would they have?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, his powers will be determined by the assignment he has received from his commander. So if a command -- if somebody has been named or appointed commander of an evacuation, then that -- it will have to be done by somebody, most often by his superior, and that superior will determine the -- the -- call it the frame or the contents of this command function, referring again to the functions of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, can a person in charge of an -- an evacuation operation issue orders, assign tasks?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, because that's -- it's an essential aspect of the command function to be able to issue taskings and assignments and normally the control function is immediately will -- connected so that he should also be in the position or will be in the position to verify the implementation of the orders he has given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, do you think, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I indicate that we will have a 20-minute break. The following break will be at about 3.25, and that will be the end of your evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you had given us a section -- a session and a half. However, as you recall, we started about two or three minutes after 1.00, so we lost, because of arguments, 30 -- approximately 32 minutes. So I would ask that we be given about approximately an hour 15 minutes which would then give us the full session and a half, probably another 15 or 20 minutes for the -- or least the half hour that we have lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have divided the time that remains after the lost half hour and reprogrammed the whole schedule. You may stretch me as far as 3.30, but not beyond that, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I just rise out of caution. I have in court with me General Pringle who has arrived today from Britain. He is the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Next witness but one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But one; my apologies. I was hoping that he could remain in Court to listen to the evidence. Out of courtesy to my learned friends, I don't know if there is any objection to that proposed course, bearing in mind they have their experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He will be permitted in court as are the other experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we were speaking about evacuation operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would the witness please be shown ERN 0467-5969. That's tab number 3 in your notebooks. It's titled, "Participation of military police in guarding prisoners of war."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I am familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the information that's contained in this document that established the regulations or principles, does this come from other military sources which were available in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. This document actually is a further specification or a further details of what is included partly in the regulations, the JNA regulations that applied to military police, as well as the 1988 regulations on the application of the international laws of war in the armed forces of the SFRY, which is also Exhibit 396 in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were the guide-lines that are in this document applicable in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, in addition to what I just explained, this particular document which is from 1993, was also advised or presented to us by a JNA witness whom we interviewed on these issues. And this witness was Colonel Radoj Paunovic, who was the commander in the 2nd Military Police Battalion in the Guards Motorised Brigade in 1991. The name is Paunovic, P-a-u-n-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, according to this document, what are the key roles or duties of the military police in guarding prisoners?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document gives a detailed description of these duties which consists of guarding the prisoners, escorting the prisoners, as well as transferring them -- to handing them over. At the pages 8, 9, 27 and 28, the document highlights the importance or the obligation, actually, to protect prisoners and to treat them humanely. And on the last, I think it's page 45, one of the last pages, there is also reference to lessons learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We would like to offer that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is one of the few documents that I wish to object to. I do not believe it has any relevance. Firstly, this is not a 65 ter document; this is a document we received later on from the OTP when the trial was already underway. Why am I raising an objection? This is a manual for a military police course, as the witness has pointed out. I will just read one sentence from the introduction. The last war-related events in the former Yugoslav republics that seceded from Yugoslavia point out the importance of the issue of prisoners of war and the need for high-level training of military police units in order to carry out these tasks. For this reason it was necessary to use the available literature from this field as well as previous experiences inside the country in order to draw up special lessons. The accompanying literature to this manual, which was produced in 1993, includes the Geneva Conventions, that is beyond dispute, I believe, as well as certain reports by experts on the treatment of prisoners of war, conditions of detention. But not the regulations, with the exception of one particular law from 1973 in relation to military prisons. What Mr. Theunens has just said was precisely the subject of one of our polemics earlier on. He quotes what was supposed to be an OTP witness but eventually wasn't. He said in relation to this 1993 manual that it was used back in 1991. Since this is a 1993 manual, and it was created for that very reason, because no such manuals were available at the time, I cannot think this manual should be used as evidence in relation to anything that occurred in 1991. We could perhaps have it marked for identification, and then if witness Paunovic eventually appears and there is other evidence to indicate that a manual like this was indeed being used back in 1991, then perhaps we could consider its admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, in the Chamber's view it will be received as a 1993 manual.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's what we're introducing as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Whether or not it has any relevance to 1991 is an obvious question, as Mr. Lukic has made very clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will become Exhibit 581.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Theunens, did the information contained in that manual exist in 1991 and earlier?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: There is exact, Your Honours, because the introduction actually mentions only that this is a dedicated lesson, there is nothing new in the lesson, it is just a dedicated one. So the information that has been pointed out in this courtroom is just an application of the Geneva Conventions in 1991, and were also valid in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the security organ. What are the duties of the security organ, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the duties of security organs and their mandate are explained in part 1 of the report, section 5, on the pages English version 77 to -- I apologise, 82. And basically their task consists of two components, counter-intelligence work and expert advice to the commander on the use of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, who does the security organ report to in a command -- in operational group, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: As in any unit where a security -- security organ is active, Your Honours, based on the JNA regulations, the security organ is subordinated to the operational commander. And at the same time maintains what is called a management relation with the military police, and has also a particular relation with security organs at the higher level and also at the subordinate level. So there are basically two chains, one subordination to the operational commander and then the security chain of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown 65 ter 395, which is tab 8. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This is the 1986 regulation on the methods and work of the security organs in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what are the functions, according to this document.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: This document actually explains how the functions are being implemented. It lists a number of procedures and operational concepts. Security organs can apply in carrying out their duties or functions and these functions are explained in the 1984 regulation, which is 6 -- excuse mu e 107 in this trial, rule of service of the security organs of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What are these functions, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: You mean this --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The earlier one?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The earlier one, it can be summarised as counter-intelligence work, expert guidance, or expert advice to the use of the military police, and this includes also a management relation with the military police and also the provision of security reporting to security organs and the security administration. Security organs at the superior command level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how was this document 65 ter 395 related to that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: As I mentioned, it explains the methods that can be used it talked about for example the use of collaborators, agents, also what I considered important for the context of this report, that security organs and the security administration can be tasked with propaganda and counter-propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could we offer that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 582, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is there anything in Exhibit 107 and this Exhibit 582 which would make you conclude whether the correction of artillery fire is a security organ function?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, there are no such entries in these two regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown ERN 0600-3049. 0600-3049. Tab 4, please. Could you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a report titled, "Security situation in the unit and the AOR," which is area of responsibility or zone of responsibility. Operations report, it has been compiled by the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade, which can be seen in the left top heading dated the 6th of November. And at the end of the document it mentions chief, Major Veselin Sljivancanin, and this document was obtained on the 18th of May from the government of Serbia and Montenegro after several attempts to obtain reports by Major Veselin Sljivancanin during the October to November 1991 time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And this report in front of you, is this the type of report that is normally filed by a security organ?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the preparation of this report I've also looked at reports that were compiled by both military commands as well as security organs outside the zone of responsibility of OG South. And for example, in the second part, under the section that discusses volunteers and paramilitaries, English page 34 there are a number of references to reports compiled by security organs of the 1st Military District or subordinate units of the 1st Military District. Most of these reports there are on the activities of an individual known under the nickname Arkan. I've also looked at a number of documents that were compiled by security organs in relation to alleged violations of the laws of war. Some of them have been exhibited in this trial with witness Agotic, I think, for example it's Exhibit 76. And this report actually discusses other issues. This Sljivancanin report, 0600-3049 is rather different from the reports I just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How is that different, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Because when we look at the contents of this document, and for example at the bottom of the first page, Sljivancanin mentions weaknesses in the system of command and the impact that has. That's actually at section at the bottom of the English version, so for the B/C/S I think it's a bit more to the top. Anyway, he starts with the discussion of the situation with Muslims and Macedonians in the guards brigade. Then he talks about weaknesses in the system of command, whereby in the English version, the bottom of the second page, Sljivancanin talks about the command situation in the 1st motorised battalion, where he says, I quote, "It is positively affected by groups from Petrova Gora detachment and other value volunteers within the composition of this battalion." Still he adds the situation is bad. And he gives a number of examples which also refer to -- or not examples, but he mention that there's a weak command and control system in the battalions, for example he says, "commands and battalions do not know what their casualties are." Now, this report, one would I'm that a critical review of command and control within the battalions would be sent to the operational group commander, i.e. to the next superior, to the superior of these battalions, but looking at this document it is actually sent, and that that can be seen on the first page. In the heading. It's sent to the security organ of the cabinet of the SSNO, so for the federal ministry for all people's, or national defence. So the report contains mainly operational information, which compared to other reports from the time, i.e., 1991, which were compiled by other security organs, appears to be significantly different by its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'd like to offer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 583, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's turn now to the powers of a security organ. Is a security organ or assistance commander for security endowed with the powers to command and issue orders?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: When we talk about assistant commander for security, we mean by that the chief of security, or the chief of security organs. According to the regulations he can only issue orders or -- give commands or issue commands to his subordinates, i.e. other officers or personnel within the security organs in his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Under what circumstances can the assistance commander of security, the chief of the security organ, issue tasks and orders, outside of his unit?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, this is under the same circumstances as described earlier, that a commander can delegate some of his powers, i.e. some of his command functions to any officer he desires to and then he this could be done a security officer who would, by such delegation, actually could become a commanding officer in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can an assistant commander for security ever be assigned to command a military operation by a commander of an operational group?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If the commander of the operational group delegates the powers to command this specific operation to a security organ, then -- or the assistance commander for security, then this assistant commander for security will become the officer in charge of this operation. And the fact that he is in charge of an operation becomes the most of -- or the only important issue then which -- whereby the fact -- whether he is a security officer or maybe a logistics officer or morale officer is -- ceases to be of importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would that include evacuation operations, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move to some issues relating to the laws of war. Are you familiar with Exhibit 396, which is regulations on the application of international laws of war and armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And this is discussed in -- in section 7 of the first part of report, together with other regulations that apply to these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, may the witness be shown Article 20 of Exhibit 396, which is on page 14, then Article 21. First, are you familiar with Article 20, please?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what is that? Or actually, could you look at Article 21 next?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Article 21 is discussed on page 127, English version, of the first part of my report. And basically it states that -- should I read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, could you just summarise what are in Article 20 and 21?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
