utterances.text: Article 20 discusses individual responsibility, individual criminal responsibility. It means that every individual of the armed forces shall be personally accountable for violations of the laws of war if you commit such a violation or orders someone to commit one. 21 deals with -- we would describe here as command responsibility, i.e. the responsibility of the commander for actions of his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do these rules apply to all officers?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that includes commanders of subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. The regulation speaks about officers, officers without specifying the nature or without adding any limitations to the concept of officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about an officer in charge of a military operation, such as an evacuation operation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Based on this regulation, the same articles would apply, as they are described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, could we turn to Article 36, which is on page 20. I'm going to read just the first sentence on page 20 of that article. "A Yugoslav officer who learns of violations of the laws of war shall order the circumstances and facts surrounding the violation be investigated and necessary evidence collected." Who does this apply to, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: According to this article from the 1988 regulations, it applies to all officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, if there is an allegation of a war crime, who were the officers most likely to investigate and arrest the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on the regulations in the JNA that apply to security organs and military police, security organs and military police would be the most -- would be the best qualified and the most experienced to carry out such activities, and later on, of course, at the later stage in the investigation, also military prosecutors intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, based on that article, if a commander is advised that a violation of war is occurring at that moment, what is his or her obligation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Based on the Article 21, he has to do everything to stop the violation from continuing. And then linked to the other articles he has to act to preserve the evidence and also have the alleged perpetrators secured or arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to 65 ter 95, which is tab 5. Page 28, which is Article 53. And what does this concern?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Article 53 of the 1985 law on the services in the armed forces. The article in its first paragraph states that any member of the armed forces is duty-bound to carry out orders issued by their superiors unless it is clear that carrying out such an order would constitute a criminal offence. In the fourth paragraph of this article it is explained what should be done if the compliance with that order would constitute a criminal offence, stating that a member of the armed forces to engage that order he receives complies with that order would constitute a criminal offence. The member of the armed forces shall immediately notify a higher superior officer or an officer senior to the individual who issued the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what if he does, in fact, contact a higher officer or a more senior officer and doesn't get a response? What is the officer to do then?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, according to this Article 53, he has to inform his immediate superior and if that doesn't work, he goes to the superior of that superior. And in the case of the guards brigade, this would mean -- because during your [indiscernible] in Vukovar they are subordinate to the 1st Military District, that first the commander of the 1st Military District would have contacted. I'm giving this example in the assumption that the order to commit the crime would have been received by the commander of the guards brigade of Operational Group South. So first of all, the commander of the 1st military district; and if that doesn't works the federal secretary for All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look at a somewhat related regulation in Exhibit 396, Article 22 at page 15.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It states the same, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that states, "A member of the armed forces shall be liable to criminal punishment also for violations of the laws of war committed by following orders resulting in the commission of a war crime or other grave criminal offence if he knew that the orders were intended to bring about a violation of the laws of war which constitutes a criminal offence." Are these types of regulations found in the regulations of armies other than the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I only know for the -- the army in which I served, the Belgian armed forces, and we have similar regulations which is quite logical because this is all a reflection of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We would like to offer 65 ter 95, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 584, Your Honours. Exhibit 684, Your Honour. No. 584, Your Honour, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Theunens, let's move on to issues relating to investigations. Have you ever performed a search for military documents of Operational Group South or the Guards Motorised Brigade in relation to investigations conducted in relation to the murders at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. From -- I arrived at ICTY end of June, 2001 and from the moment I was assigned so this case I have both looked within the archives of the OTP for such documents, as well as drafted several requests for assistance to Serbia and Montenegro in order to obtain such documents or other documents that relate to the discipline situation in OG South. I can provide the details for these requests, if necessary. And so far -- I mean the only documents I came across, and the only documents we received are the ones included in the second part of the report, section 3, from the pages 121 to 124, in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a document from Serbia and Montenegro, any documents, in response to your requests?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: You mean specifically for -- for violations of the laws of war or in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, in relation to any investigation which occurred at Ovcara, in relation to Operational Group South or the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, what I remember the only -- sorry for the transcript. In the package of documents we received in response to other requests, there was one order, it's the order 471-2 from OG south, which is 424, which mentions the word "investigation," sorry it's an operational report, not an order, 471-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in Exhibit 424, which is this report you're speaking of, is there any mention of an investigation in relation to the deaths at Ovcara in that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit mentions the arrival of an investigation team and also discusses its composition, but it doesn't mention anything in relation to Ovcara. I think it also talks about clearing up the battlefields, but that's the farthest it goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, is there any mention of a crime that had occurred at Ovcara in that document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, there isn't, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, may the witness please be shown 65 ter 611, which is tab number 6 at page 3. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This is an -- I mean, the article I used in my report in English page 122 is an excerpt from the so-called bulletin or Bultin [phoen] which was a publication compiled and distributed by the federal Ministry of Defence or all people -- All People's Defence in SFRY at the time. And this article is a statement by the command of the 1st army or 1st military district, and it -- from the 2nd of December, 1991. Discussing the arrival and activities of the investigation team, which is actually mentioned in Exhibit 424, and also it mentions the focus of its activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what is the focus of its activities?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: From the last paragraph, the second paragraph in this article, it can be seen that the focus of the investigation is actually -- are actually what is described as the Croatian paramilitary formations. And -- yes, indeed, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'd like to offer this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 585, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As there is no mention of Ovcara in that exhibit, have you reviewed any 1991 military documents relating to an investigation occurring as to the murders at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, there are many documents compiled by the Croatian authorities, but because I couldn't verify the reliability of these documents or the credibility of the sources they quoted, I decided not to use them for this report. My -- I preferred to have JNA or SFRY documents. And, as I mentioned, there have been several requests to Serbia and Montenegro, but so far, without many results. I mean results we obtained are included in the report. So to answer the question, I have not been in the position to verify -- to review other 1991 JNA military documents, because we have not managed to obtain them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown 65 ter 605, which is tab 9 in your notebooks. Could you tell us what this document is and what it concerns?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an unsigned statement in English by the office of the military prosecutor of the VJ, so the structure that succeeded to the JNA, dated the 25th of November, 1992 entitled, "Information on crimes against humanity and international law committed in the territory of the former SFRY and processed by military courts." It is discussed on pages 123, 124 on -- in the English version of my report, the second part. And basically it states that prosecution efforts are focused against or on the members of the Croatian armed forces, and it shows, it has a conclusion, and I quote, "Evidence shows that war crimes and the crime of genocide were committed almost exclusively by members of the armed forces of Croatia while members of the armed forces of the SFRY complied with the norms of international humanitarian law, both with respect to parties in the armed conflict and the civilian population."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's on page 2?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, is there any mention in this document about crimes that occurred in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, there isn't, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is there any mention of an investigative team conducting an investigation in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, there isn't, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Any mention of an investigation team ever conducted an investigation in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'd offer that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 586.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You got there before I did. I wanted to object to this document being admitted for purely formal reasons. We don't know who produced this document, when it was produced, why it was produced, who it was produced by. There is no seal on it. We have nothing on that. We need to identify the document properly first and see what it's about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: His comments that will go to weight. It is received in evidence, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown 65 ter 219, which is tab 7. It's a letter to Slobodan Milosevic and General Adzic from Helsinki Watch, a committee of Human Rights Watch. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this letter and the annex consists of an overview of what U.S. Helsinki Watch describes as violations of the laws of war and other war crimes committed by -- or allegedly committed by -- actually it's called -- I'm sorry, "Human rights abuses by the Serbian government and Yugoslav army forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is there any reference to the murders at Vukovar in this document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. On the page -- the English version ERN 0018-7370.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's page 7, sir.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed. At the top of the page mention is made of alleged crimes that were committed in Vukovar on or after the 18th of November. And I don't know whether you wish me to read it out, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you read the paragraph out, please. It's only one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: "The City of Vukovar was under constant siege by Serbian forces for three months. When the city fell on November 18 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you slow down for the translators, please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: So "when the city fell on November 18, 15.000 people who were in the fled from the fighting emerged from the basements in which though lived for 12 weeks. After Vukovar's fall civilians and soldiers of the combat were beaten or arrested by Serbian paramilitary groups and the JNA. On the basis of interviews with displaced persons from Vukovar and foreign journalists and humanitarian workers who visited Vukovar immediately after its fall, Helsinki Watch has reason to believe that many Croatian men, both civilians and combatants who had laid down their arms were summarily executed by Serbian forces after Vukovar's fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether the government of Serbia and Montenegro responded to this?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my report, second part, the English page 123, subparagraph 3 between brackets, I mentioned the letter, the chief of cabinet of president of Serbia, Milosevic, sent to human rights -- to Helsinki Watch, acknowledging the reception of the letter and the report attached to it. And this is based on 65 ter number 220.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'd like to offer that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 587, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to move to an issue of town commanders. What was the purpose of a town commander?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, town commands are discussed in part 2 of my report, English pages 109 to 100 -- I have to look. 119, I apologise. Based on the documents from 1st Military District, OG South, and I mean by this orders and reports dating from the end of September to end of November 1991 time period. And also instructions we obtained from the government from Serbia and Montenegro in response to requests for assistance that were drafted for this purpose, [Realtime transcript read in error "."] town commands carried out all duties of administration and authority, which would normally be carried out by civilian authorities. And I apologise, but it's actually a continuation of the sentence, so there should be a comma after "purpose" in the transcript. It's a bit of a long sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And why are they needed, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Because -- they are needed because in the conditions of war, I mean armed conflict, and again I base this only on the documents that I have been able to study, in particular the orders issued by Zivota Panic, commander of the 1st Military District. Because there were no bodies of civil authorities in the area of the zone of responsibility of OG South, or according to Panic, no such bodies which were able to carry out his powers, the military had to fill this gap. And we see for example that, if I'm not wrong, in October, officers, including a security officer of OG South, Vukasinovic, is appointed as a town commander. Vukasinovic, town commander in Negoslavci. Now, after the fall of Vukovar of the 18th of November we see that there is an -- additional orders being issued and for example that Colonel Milorad Vojnovic is appointed commander of the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown 65 ter 933 and then 65 ter 934, which are tab 10 and 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with these two documents, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I'm familiar with these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do they describe the duties of a town commander?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, these documents actually describe the duties of the organs for civilian affairs of a JNA command in the crisis areas. The first 65 ter number 933 refers to the SSNO instruction 588-1, which dates from the 27th of November, 1991. And then the second one, 588-3, is actually a clarification of the fourth point of 588-1. And dates, if I'm not wrong, from the 6th of December. And they are discussed on the pages 115 to 119 in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what are these documents discuss, just briefly what each one mentions and discusses?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: They discuss the importance of the establishment of bodies of civilian authority, as well as the cooperation that the JNA has to show towards these bodies, and before cooperation, of course, the assistance to establish them, and that covers all aspects, not only authority but also security; several times mention is made of the requirement to protect the civilian population of abuses. It also mentions the role of town commands in case there are no civilian authorities and related issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'd like to offer both documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 588 and 589, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, if there is a town commander and there are also military units located within the town, is the town commander in command and control of those units?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, from a review of in particular the orders and reports of the 1st Military District and operation group south, covering the October/November time period, it is clear that there is the -- that these are two separate issues. A town commander has no authority or no command over the units there, unless they are his own units. Because from what I've seen, town command is actually an additional function that an officer will carry out in addition to his normal duties, unless it is specified that he is replaced by somebody else for his normal duties. I haven't seen a document where the fact of being a town commander is the exclusive task of that officer, and I mean by this documents dating from prior to the 23rd of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, if there is a town commander and within the town an evacuation operation is occurring, does that place the town commander in charge of that operation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I will try to be brief, Your Honours. As I mentioned earlier, the orders and documents I have seen from the 1st Military District and OG South in relation to town commanders do not mention any operational responsibilities for these people, for these town commanders, and this also includes evacuation operations. Again, going back to the doctrine, which we discussed earlier, and talking about operations, there is no requirement -- or it would make no sense for a town commander to be involved or to become involved in an evacuation operation or any other operation that is commanded by somebody else. Because this would actually represent a violation of the principle of single authority. Of course, if the commander, i.e. the person who is superior to both the commander of the evacuation and the town commander issues any particular orders, for example, for the evacuation commander to coordinate with the town commander, then of course then there will be an exchange of information or coordination between both. But -- but that doesn't mean -- I mean it's certainly not to be confounded with the town commander becoming involved in command aspects of the evacuation operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when is a town commander's function completed, or when does his role as town commander end?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on the documents of Operational Group South and the 1st Military District, and I mean by this orders and reports, I am not in a position to answer this question. However, Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem were not the only areas where town commanders were established, and in my report there is a document included from -- that applies to Western Slavonia, the town of Okucani, and this is an order by General Talic, Momir Talic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to 65 ter 937?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's tab 12, please. Tab 12 in your notebooks. And what does that document indicate?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: So this Momir Ordavir [phoen], and I see that there is an error in the report. It says Furir Rekman [phoen], Krajina Corps, but it didn't exist then yet. It should be the 5th JNA Corps. I apologise. Talic states that "because the civilian authorities are operating and able to carry out their duties, the town command can be disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could we offer this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will become Exhibit 590, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may be slightly late with this, but I'm not sure what this document has to do with the territory covered by the indictment. The document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's not tendered as a geographically relevant document, but I would understand is an indication of what does happen. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's just get back to that document for a moment. That order says, "The civil authorities of Okucani municipality, having been fully established in discharging all their governing functions, thus overriding the need for any further existence of the Okucani town command, and they disband the town command." Now, sir, what does that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it indicates, as I explained, that at least in Okucani, which was from the purely conceptual point of view, if I could explain it like that, quite similar to other areas in Croatia where an armed conflict had taken place, that the order to disband, or that the town command continues to exist, or it exists as long as there are no civilian bodies who are able of carrying out the tasks of civilian authority and administration in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move to our final issue. Personnel records. In 1991 do you know whether the JNA maintained personnel records for its soldiers?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, like any armed force I'm familiar, the JNA maintained personnel records for its personnel. So not only soldiers, but also non-commissioned officers and offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We're going to be dealing with the next three tabs. And let's start with tab 13, which is 65 ter 455. Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an except of the personnel file or personnel records of Mile Mrksic. And this one, this excerpt or this section deals with the assignments he held as an officer in the JNA and subsequently the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about his assignments in relation to the Guards Motorised Brigade as indicated on this document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: From page 2, actually, the second page, it is obvious that Mile Mrksic served already from 1968 in the -- in what was called then the guards brigade, and he continued to be assigned to the guards brigade until the 30th of June, carrying out different duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What positions did he hold between July 1999, 2000 and June 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to the entries on page 5 on the English translation, Mile Mrksic with a rank of colonel was commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade. The A stands for the level of -- I would call professionalisation. There were three levels of unit, A, B, C, whereby A has the most professional, C the least as to mobilisation, on the 11th of December, 1991, Mile Mrksic is promoted major-general but remains according to his records commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade. On the 30th of June, 1992, Major-General Mile Mrksic is command -- is appointed commander to the corps special units, [B/C/S spoken], KSJ, which was a newly-established -- I wouldn't call unit, but corps, established in -- sometimes in -- I think in June or July 1992. Consisting of a number of, call it, elite units like the 63rd airborne brigade or parachute brigades, the 72nd, I think, assault and strike brigade, if I'm not wrong. There was also a particular protection regiment, as well as the guards brigade. So the guards brigade is included in this special forces corps, KSJ, and Major-General Mile Mrksic remains commander of the special forces corps, according to this entry in his records, until the 16 of September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There doesn't appear to be any mention of Operational Group South. Why is that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wouldn't know so. All I can say is that when I looked through these records, on another page which is further on, actually, it's -- it bears the number 5, but I don't -- I'm not sure you will find it. It's actually 0422-2854. It says that it's a descriptive assessment of the way how Major-General Mrksic accomplished his duties. I don't know whether it's visible for all of you, but in the second paragraph it says that the, "In the Vukovar operation 1991 he" -- i.e. Mrksic, "commanded the Operative Group South." So my understanding is that these temporary assignments are not included in the first section of the document we discussed, but will be included in other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could we offer that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 591, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter 456 which is tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what are these records, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are the -- this is an excerpt of the personnel records for Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when does it indicate he was a member of the guards brigade, Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: When we go to the page 0361-8848. It mentions the guards brigade, and the earliest date I can find there is 1972. But I think more relevant in the context of my report is that Sljivancanin, or Veselin Sljivancanin as a major was commander of the 1st military police battalion of the Guards Motorised Brigade from 1988 or 1989, and there are other duties. And then he is head of the security organs from the 12th of August 1991. In the record it says PPK, which stands for [B/C/S spoken], lieutenant-colonel. But my understanding is that he was only appointed end of November lieutenant-colonel. And this is on the page 0361-8849. He -- he stays in the guards brigade until the -- at least the 18th of October, 1993. No, excuse me, until the 5th of October, 1993, I apologise. 5th of October, 1993. Whereby, after having been chief of the security organs or assistant commander for security, he is appointed Deputy Commander or Chief of Staff of the guards brigade and as it mentions at the bottom of the page, guards brigade being a unit of the corps for special units of the VJ. And the date for this start of this assignment is the 2nd of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May we offer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 592, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, sir, 65 ter 457, tab 15. Could you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is -- again this is an excerpt from the personnel record of Miroslav Radic. But I don't think it's the right one to be able to draw conclusions as to the duties he accomplished in 1991. We should have another section for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to react in a timely manner this time around. The document that we have on our screens now, 03618369 was one of the documents on the 65 ter list. The other document that the expert has referred to, is probably the document that ends with the following two digits: 90. This was served on us this morning. It's a military document, but it was not on the 65 ter list. And no additional explanations were offered. We have not had sufficient time to familiarise ourselves with this. But we do not wish to nitpick all the same. Can this be just evidence, please, and not actually evidence [as interpreted]? The dead-line should have been a lot of earlier, but it is not my intention to object anyway. Anyway, the 65 ter list, this other document that the witness has spoken about was never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was the wrong pages within the Radic personnel file. The correction pages were disclosed on June 15th, 2006. And the correct number is ERN is 0361-8390.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying these are the correct pages, the earlier ones were the wrong ones, but both come from the same source document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which is the personnel record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In those circumstances, Mr. Borovic, this will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 593, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was disclosed to us some hours ago. The dead-line for all military documents is normally 48 hours, and the same thing should apply to this one, too, this is an entirely different document and an entirely different photograph and an entirely different personnel file. But if the Chamber is pleased ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, if you think the photograph is of another officer, when you cross-examine tomorrow we can discover that. The other information in there ought to be known to your client in a flash, if it's his personal record. So I do not imagine that you would be embarrassed by the document if it really is his record. If it's not, that can emerge from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us when the defendant Radic was a member of the guards brigade, according to his personnel records?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I don't have the document in front of me. It's difficult for me to read from the monitor, but at least I know on the page 0361-8393 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One moment. One moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at the page 8393 this gives an overview of the military career and the assignments held by Miroslav Radic, and according to the top entry he joined the Guards Motorised Brigade in 1985. In any event, according to this document in -- on the 24th of May, 1990, and this is the -- the fifth line, Radic became commander of the 3rd motorised company in the 1st motorised battalion of the Guards Motorised Brigade. And he held that post until the 15th of July, 1992. Whereupon, on the 16th he became Deputy Commander of the 1st Military Police Battalion of the Guards Motorised Brigade. And then the next entry, which refers to the 25th of August, 1992, Radic still Deputy Commander of a military police battalion, but this time in the 46th regiment for security in the corps for -- for special units of the VJ, so the unit which is under the command or the corps which is under the command of Major-General Mrksic until summer 1993, but it's not clear from the record here how long Radic [as interpreted] stays in the 46th regiment or protection regiment -- excuse me, the 46th protection regiment in the corps for special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'd like to offer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It has already been received, Mr. Weiner. Exhibit 593.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Weiner, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Weiner. Thank you very much. You're 3.31. We'll now [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, we'd better wait for your clients and a witness. So I won't start the clock running now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens. I hope the interpreters can hear me well. It seems that the mic is a bit too far away, but I'll try to proceed carefully. Mr. Theunens, based on your CV, I can see that you are commander, third class [as interpreted], in Belgium. Could you describe it to us in terms of the JNA system, could you give us the equivalent in the JNA system?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mistake in the transcript. I said that Mr. Theunens was commander OE 3. OF 3.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the rank is commandant which a rank between captain and major. The OF 3 stands for the NATO equivalent because I understand in most western militaries there is not such a rank as commandant, except maybe in the navy, but then you're talking about somebody who is much more senior. Now, I wouldn't dare to draw an equivalent to the JNA, because I'm well aware that there were captains first class in the JNA. But my understanding of comparing the JNA to any other -- any NATO military would be that the JNA was very much of a top-down system, whereby lower ranking officers, like lieutenant, captain or maybe a captain first class, would certainly not be encouraged to make as such initiative as is the case in NATO militaries. But to come back to the Belgian system, even though it is equivalent to a NATO major, I mean the rank of commandant, it is still a junior officer rank whereby -- in Belgium at least whereby the next rank major is considered a senior officer rank. So I don't know whether this clarifies enough for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Theunens. Based on your CV, I can see that at one point you started working for the intelligence and Security Service of the Belgian army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. I was actually appointed to start to work there. It was not my own choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I didn't say it was by your own choice, but I'd like to know what tasks you had within that service from 1992 onwards when you stayed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, because according to the transcript it seems that I stayed in the former Yugoslavia since 1992, which is not correct. So could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I made a mistake. Did you perhaps stay in the former Yugoslavia from 1994 on? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for the clarification now. I started to work in the Belgium intelligence security service in 1992 as an intelligence analyst. When I was sent to the UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb in 1994, I started to work there as a military information officer, and it is obvious that while working for the United Nations, I did not maintain any contacts except for administrative purposes with my previous office. I was in Zagreb as a UN officer, and not as a Belgian officer. And the same applies to my mission with UNTAES in Vukovar from July 1996 to April 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, Mr. Theunens. Please tell me, throughout this period of time, did you also send reports to your intelligence service back in Belgium?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a law on secrecy in Belgium, and I mean my CV, I think, is very brief on what I did in Belgium. I don't mind answering the question, but I'm not supposed to provide these answers to people who are not the right to have these answers, so it puts me in a problematic situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will you be able to answer yes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's enough for your purposes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Based on CV I can see that at one point in 1998 and 1999 you were also head of an intelligence cell within the Belgian service covering the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, the information in my CV is clear, it was a national intelligence cell with the SFOR headquarters, and I can mention what is there. If there -- I don't -- I mean, if there is a good -- a requirement for more information, I would prefer to have that in closed session. But I feel -- I mean, the formulation of the question is not exactly a reflection of what I did. I think what is in my CV is a more correct reflection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that in 2001 you became a full-time employee of the OTP here in The Hague; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours, but I'm still a member of the Belgian armed forces, i.e. I have been seconded to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. However, when you came here, when you were hired by the OTP, you had to sign a contract stating that in consideration for certain remuneration you were to provide services within the military analysis team; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the way how this question is formulated depicts -- I mean, depicts me as some kind of a mercenary or so. I have been hired by the ICTY, by the OTP, to do a certain job, which is in accordance with the job description I have received. And this consider -- this covers mainly military analysis. I -- "provide services", for me, has a negative connotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, none of us here are mercenaries, naturally all of us work for money. I just wanted to establish whether you are on the payroll of the OTP or whether you are being paid by the Belgian army.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I'm paid by the OTP, but how naive it may look, money is not my -- the only motive in my life, and certainly not the only motive to be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By coming to the OTP you also accepted to support the activities of the OTP aimed at prosecuting individuals who had committed war crimes which feel within -- which fall within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean you -- aimed at prosecuting individuals who had committed war crimes. I mean, I'm not a lawyer, but it first has to be proven whether they have committed war crimes or not, and of course I'm requested to -- to collect and analyse information, but I see it more as a job in the assistance of justice than merely the prosecution of individuals. Of course I work for the OTP, but as you will see from this report, and also from the requests that were sent to Serbia and Montenegro, the main purpose of the report is to describe a particular aspect, in this case the activities or the operations of Operations Group South, and it's up to the people who use this report, be it in the Prosecution, the Defence or the Honourable Judges, to see what they will do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. When signing the contract to work with the OTP, you also accepted a duty not to reveal any secrets that you learn of when working for the OTP, especially not those secrets that could compromise the basic line of work of the OTP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I think there is -- I mean two aspects to this question. What kind of secrets are you talking about? It's obvious that I'm not -- I will not discuss certain -- I mean, the procedures of our work with people who have no need to know, but on the other hand, looking at the other aspect, what I understand is your question, if, for example, I come across material known as Rule 68, it is my duty to not only -- not only inform the legal staff in my team about it, or in the case team I'm working in, but also make sure that this material is made available to -- yeah, to those interested, including the Defence. So I'm not so clear what you mean by "secrets."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Does this mean that in a situation where you learn of some material which falls under Rule 68, if somebody were to put a question to you pertaining to that, you would be able to disclose that information even though such material had not yet been closed to the Defence by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question. I mean when I -- let's take the request for assistance that was sent -- that have been sent to Serbia and Montenegro since 2002. Whenever we get a reply, it first has to be put in the system that takes maximum a week, then it is disclosed, I don't have to wait for question from somebody, I inform, I notify the legal team, the lawyers on my team that this and this material has arrived, I need to look at the material with a language assistant, but independent of the context -- of the contents, it will be disclosed, and certainly, if it's Rule 68. So I don't understand your reference that I have to wait for a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify it for you. If I were to ask you, what would you do in a situation where here, under oath, you were supposed to state in front of the Trial Chamber what you know about exculpatory material in a situation where such material has not yet been disclosed to the Defence by the OTP. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: And do you mean by this material discovered by me or related to me or what is the purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Material about which you, as an employee of the OTP and an expert, know something?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I must say I -- I mean material I'm familiar with which could be considered Rule 68 will be disclosed. I -- there would be no alternative. And I mean by material, documents, because I mainly deal with documentary evidence, whereby it's in my responsibility to, based on the taskings I have received from my team leader or the senior trial attorney, to identify such material within the evidence that is available at the OTP, or by writing request to, in most cases for this particular situation, Serbia and Montenegro, or any other country or organisation that may have the information we are interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you this: Within the scope of your work, you work as an analyst within a service within the OTP. So therefore, within that framework, is your work guided by the findings you receive from a prosecutor on your team, or are you independent in your research?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Actually, I mean I would -- I would hope to be entirely independent, and I mean by that, that I would have access to all information that was available in 1991 and that was produced in relation to these events, and I mean by this, mainly military documents. But the main handicap I have had since starting this report and that was sometime in 2003, there have been interruptions, was the lack of assistance, or the lack of response from Serbia and Montenegro to requests we sent, requests for documents, both orders as well as reports by the 1st Military District and Operational Group South. And again, if you want, I can give you detailed overview of the material we requested, which clearly covered Rule 68 aspects, but where we were -- said it doesn't exist, even though it had been present at other times by other parties in the trial. Now, coming back to the Prosecutor, the Prosecutor asks me questions, he can give me taskings, but he will not -- or he cannot order me what to write. Because that's -- I mean, maybe I can explain the analysis -- the intelligence cycle and also describe how analysts work, but in a nutshell, an analyst looks at information, collects information, analyses it, and then comes with conclusions. It's not the opposite, it's not that there is a conclusion and then there is a task or methodology, I wouldn't call it methodology, but kind of manipulation to select the information that suits the conclusion. I think it would be very unprofessional to work like that, and since having worked -- I have worked as an analyst since 1992, I've never received such a tasking, i.e. to come with information that supports certain pre-conceived ideas, and I haven't received such a tasking here either; on the contrary. And I would invite you to, if you really -- I mean, looking at your question, to look at the report and to look at sections which are not supported by official documentation, be it from the JNA or the SFRY or other documentation from parties that were involved on the JNA side in the conflict in Vukovar in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Before compiling your expert report, Mr. Theunens, were you actively included in giving advice, were you actively involved in giving advice to the Prosecutor when the indictment in this case was drafted? And amended.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the initial indictment, I think, dates from 1996. I arrived in 2001, but it is correct that I was involved in the drafting of amendments to the indictment whereby my involvement was limited to giving military advice, which consisted of making sure that the terminology, military terminology that was used was correct and accurate reflection of the evidence we had. It is obvious, because I am not a lawyer or a jurist, I did not get involved in legal aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, can you tell us whether, within your research, while preparing this expert report, you came across some relevant material that could be used under Rule 68, but you chose not to include it in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the report was closed in August or was finished in August 2005. The material -- Rule 68 material that was discovered before was disclosed and/or included in the report. It could well be that Rule 68 material that was discovered then was just disclosed but not included in the report. That's possible, because there are certain limitations to the report. For what material is concerned that was obtained after August 2005, obviously the report was closed, it was not included in the report, but as far as I know it was disclosed. When I say "as far as I know," I mean by that that I informed senior trial attorney and the case manager about the contents of the material, i.e. that it was Rule 68 and the requirement to disclose it. I admit that I have not verified that it was disclosed, but there's only so much one can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. You mentioned certain limitations. Can you tell us what they entail, what kinds of limitations existed when this material was included in your expert report. I'm now referring to the material you mentioned dating from August 2005.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The biggest limitation I noticed, and that's actually included in the last page of the section, "Scope and overview" of the report is that a number of documents that we considered relevant for the preparation of this study, and were therefore requests from Serbia and Montenegro and I mentioned reports from the previous years, the requests were from 2002, they were not available at the time of the filing of this report. I want to emphasise is among these documents is what I would assume are Rule 68 material because we requested for example, reports by then Colonel Mrksic about the disciplinary situation with the volunteers. We requested reports by the security organs of the Guards Motorised Brigade including -- so, OG South, not only Major Sljivancanin, but also Major Vukasinovic, Captain Karanfilov, other officers of the security organs. And we were said such reports do not exist. We requested the personal notebooks of Colonel Mrksic, Major Sljivancanin and Captain Radic, we receive as reply these documents do not exist in the archives of Serbia and Montenegro, nor in the archives of the guards brigade. Whereas based on the information obtained from other JNA officers or former JNA officers, we know that such documents should be in the archives. Now that, I must admit, was a frustrating thing because I believe that the work of the ICTY is about justice, it's not about winning trials at any price, because otherwise I wouldn't be here. I mean, an intelligence analyst looks at information, and the more information he or she has, the better job he or she can do. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Tell me, please, what kind of limitations existed in relation to this material that you received in August but did not include in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: There is no specific limitation to -- I mean whether we received it in August or not, as an analyst you're making a selection of material, not a selection to arrive just at stuff that is handy to have because it would have been disclosed to you anyway. So if I would have been extremely selective, in a sense that I would only include, between brackets, incriminating information, I'm pretty sure that you would highlight it during your cross-examination, so I think when you go through the report there is no indication whatsoever of such a selection. It is true, but I wouldn't consider the limitation that this report does not talk about the activities of the Croatian side, because - why? - well, it's not a conflict analysis; it is a study of Operational Group South. I mean, the information that was obtained after August 2005, it was envisaged to prepare some kind of an addendum, but because of the unpredictable nature of the timing of receiving this material, normally request for assistance, there are 30 days to reply. There are documents you obtain with two years delay. Some -- we still obtain documents like the 18th of May. The first ever document we received which is drafted by Major Sljivancanin, even though the first requests dates from the 6th of December, 2002, therefore, for those reasons, it was decided not prepare an addendum, but to disclose these documents upon their arrival, and also to tender them during my examination. So I'm not aware of any other limitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Theunens. Just to wrap up this particular set of questions. Who do you answer to for the quality and effectiveness of your work with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Within the military analysis team there is a team leader, and obviously he is kept aware of the quality or the lack of quality of my work through his contacts with the senior trial attorneys I work for. Since my -- since the start of my work at the ICTY or at the OTP, I've worked for several cases, and so I understand or I assume that the team leader has contacts with the senior trial attorneys that are responsible for those cases. Now, I'm just -- to continue, I'm not very clear what you mean by the word "effectiveness." What do you mean by the word "effectiveness" of my work?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for asking this. I'm glad to clarify. Every job requires certain qualifications to do well. Another thing is, to put these qualifications to some good use in the most effective way in the shortest possible time for the greatest possible effect.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean such a definition would, in my view, apply to a salesman or something -- somebody, who at the end of the month has to come with his sales figures. I think it's very hard to measure the effectiveness of the work of -- of people who are not in an economic or another sector or in a trade sector or something. Yeah, I mean there's not much more I can add to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Theunens. Everybody keeps reminding us here in this courtroom of the importance of being effective, especially time effective. Starting with the Chamber and then on to the registrar. That is why I wanted to ask you about being effective. Let's move on to something different now. I now want to move on to your report. In the introduction to your report, you state the methodology that you used in producing this report. That is on page 1, right? You had the opportunity, when creating this expert opinion, to attend witness interviews, to talk to some of the witnesses, and during these interviewing and proofings to be actively involved. In some cases you saw statements that were given to OTP investigators. Would that seem to be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It's correct, Your Honour. But maybe it's a translation issue, but I don't think this is an expert opinion. I don't express opinions in this report. This report is an overview of documentation and analysis of documentation, whereby the nature of the documentation has been explained in the introductory section of the report, i.e. SFRY legislation, military orders and document -- and reports from the SSNO, 1st Military District and OG South. And also some open-source material, both from official sources like the SSNO, as well as from other parties that were involved in the conflict on the side of the JNA, if I could describe it like that. I may be not very effective with these long answers but I wanted to clarify that. It is correct that I have been involved in witness interviews in proofing sessions, I have also sat here in court when military witnesses testified. But there is not one entry in this report that is based on witness statement. And that's also clearly indicated in the introductory section.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, Mr. Theunens. As far as this is concerned, as far as the fact is concerned that you do not invoke any witness statements or anything that you heard during interviews that you may have attended. However, while producing this report you did use information that you learned at trials, and thus perhaps indirectly you included such information in your report.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the only information in relation to trials I include in this report is a reference to the Belgrade special court Ovcara trial, whereby I -- I think I mentioned a reference to the indictment there, but just to list names of the people who were indicted and that's somewhere at the end of my report, the second part, on the pages 100 -- on page 128 of my report, but unless I have forgotten something, I'm not aware of any other reference to a trial in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to be crystal clear about this, can you please go to page 3 of your analysis, the heading is, "Overview." The first sentence of the last paragraph on that page, page 3, under the heading, "Overview." This is at the beginning of your report. Have you got that, sir? This is -- it starts on page 2, the heading "overview," and then if you could please turn the page, go to page 3, and then the last paragraph, the first sentence, you give us the basis for your analysis here. Could you please read the relevant portion out to us, sir. Thank you. For the interpreters, again page 3 of the introduction in the B/C/S, last paragraph, first sentence.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I hope I have the right sentence, but it reads as follows: "This analysis is based on a study of documents in possession of the OTP with the exception of witness/suspect statements and court testimony." So the exception covers both witness and suspect statements, as well as court testimony. Do you want me to continue or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, thank you. That was precisely the reason I asked you the question. You said that no witness statements were used for your report. But you do not exclude the possibility of using the substance of what you learned at various trials or witness proofings or interviews. You do not rule out the possibility that you used the substance of what you may have heard for your report. Would that seem to be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's an incorrect assessment, because the reference is the footnote in the report all refer to -- to documents, and I've described the -- the type of documents. Discussing witness statements, I think it has been very useful for me to be present at interviews of witnesses, because you know as well as I do that this included also Defence witnesses, and I don't think that these people had any particular interest in coming up with a version that would be particularly favourable to the OTP or express any other bias. I think it really assisted me in -- in understanding the functioning of the JNA, SFRY armed forces and OG South in a better way. And it also guided me in identifying material that was useful for the report. But again, these were -- most of these witnesses were actually Defence witnesses, so I don't think that there is a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just one clarification, please. You say these were Defence witnesses. Does that mean that you spoke to them as Defence witnesses?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have said it included Defence witnesses, and these Defence witnesses were interviewed as any other witness is being -- is interviewed. So there were no particular, as far as I know, conditions. I do remember that when some of these witnesses were interviewed that I think it was in 2003 it happened in the VJ Dom, there was also an observer of the VJ present, but she left after two days. So that's the only particularity, I mean -- I mean, I can mention about these interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you to look at page 2. The same reference in the B/C/S. This is the page under the heading, "Overview." Fourth paragraph. You talk about the application of the rules in the armed forces of the SFRY in connection with the international laws of war. Do you mean about the rules that actually existed in writing, or which rules are you referring to here? Were there any rules or regulations that applied to a situation of armed conflict, regulation that is were actually being used back in 1991 that applied?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you will see in section 7 of part 1 of the report starting on page 122 until I think it's 128, excuse me, 147, actually. There were several regulations within -- that applied to the SFRY armed forces in 1991 which established the obligations of the SFRY armed forces to abide by the laws of armed conflict and the customs of armed conflict. First of all, there are articles in the 1982 All People's Defence law which make it mandatory for any member of the SFRY armed forces to abide by these regulations. We discussed earlier in examination Article 53 of the 1985 law on the service in the armed forces. There is also Exhibit 396, the 1988 regulations on the application of international laws of war in the armed forces of the SFRY. There may be other regulations, but at least those are the ones I used, together with the laws on military courts and military prosecutors, I used to draft this report, in particular section 7 of the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll return to some of these laws at a later stage, but now I understand what is at stage. In the next chapter of your report you say that you were given the task to compare the situation that preceded the armed clashes in Croatia in order to show the evolution of tasks pertaining to the armed forces of the SFRY during the conflict in Croatia, the intention being to show that the operations to take Vukovar were part of a more general framework of JNA operations in the summer and autumn of 1991. Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It may be a translation issue, but I was not given the task to compare the situation. I actually decided that myself, and I will express myself in a better way. I believe that the regulations that have been discussed in part 1 of the report, which describe the theoretical framework, assist in understanding what the SFRY armed forces are, what they were doing, what they were not doing, and to which regulations, or which regulations they were bound to follow, in particular when it comes to the application of the laws and customs of war. Part 1 should also assist in understanding how command and control were exercised in the SFRY armed forces. Part 2 then tries to analyse how all these regulations were implemented, and it is correct that the first section in part 2 discusses the evolution of the mission and objectives of the SFRY armed forces during the conflict in Croatia. Because I had the understanding or I came to the understanding as an analyst when looking at all the material, that based on the sources I reviewed, the SFRY armed forces did not implement the mission as it had been defined, for example, in the 1974 constitution and the 1982 All People's Defence law. During the conflict in Croatia, more specifically or in particular during the latter half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. We'll come that later about the commission and the constitutional powers of the JNA. In order to carry out such a comprehensive analysis and in order to carry out this task, which you explained a moment ago, you had to have an overview across the whole territory that your report was to refer to. This would have been a prerequisite for any conclusions that you may have drawn, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. I mean I -- as you -- as I mentioned earlier, I testified in the Milosevic case in 2004, and the tasking I had received for the report I had to compile for that case obviously looked at the entire territory of -- of the Republic of Croatia, but also to Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I had knowledge about the aspects of the conflict relevant for this report from my work for that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Theunens. When did the armed clashes first erupt in the Republic of Croatia then, and which precise parties were involved? Who started this?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe I should have explained that when I discussed my report for the Milosevic case, I have never been tasked to put together a conflict analysis whereby origin and causes and similar aspects would be investigated and analysed. My task for -- in the Milosevic case consisted of identifying the forces that were involved on the JNA side in certain geographic areas in Croatia, as well as the relations between the forces that were involved in the geographic areas and the JNA, both from the command and control aspect, as well as from logistical and other aspects covering the time period from 1991 until May 1992. I've come across information on -- on origins and cause of the conflict, but that was not subject of my analysis and it's not part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A while ago you said that in your opinion the JNA did not act in compliance with the powers granted it by the constitution, and the relevant laws. My question to you is, how could you have drawn a conclusion like that on the role and position of the armed forces without first familiarising yourself with the chronology of the events in the territory where these armed forces were operating, you don't know who was fighting who. You didn't know who the aggressor was, you didn't know how the conflict first started. In the absence of all these facts and all -- and this particular knowledge, how can you be in a position to assess the intentions of a party to this conflict?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's -- it's slightly misleading to describe this as being my opinion. As you see in section 1 of the -- the second part of the report, evolution of the mission and objectives of the SFRY armed forces, an important part of that section discusses the book of Veljko Kadijevic. Of course, from an analytical point of view it would be preferable to have the authentic documents instead of a book, but I wish to remind the Trial Chamber that Veljko Kadijevic was the then, through 1991, federal secretary for people's defence, which can be compared to a minister of defence whereby he had much wider competencies than a minister of defence -- it's -- maybe even would have. And it is exactly Kadijevic who describes the change in the mission and all the other aspects that Mr. Vasic has attributed to me. So what I -- I only quoted Kadijevic and tried to find JNA documentation that corroborated or first of all JNA documentation on those events to find out who was right. And this is then reflected in the first section of my report. So it is just a reflection of official documentation and Kadijevic's book. It's not my opinion. And I wish to add - sorry - also statements Kadijevic and Adzic made during that time period, public statements, which were published as -- as official points of view of, in this case, Kadijevic, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When talking about Mr. Veljko Kadijevic's book, or any statements that he made, my belief is precisely that his book was not tantamount to evidence under oath. This was, after all, a man who was never called to testify anywhere, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not aware whether Kadijevic or Adzic ever testified about what happened or didn't happen, but if a minister of defence publishes a book which is a clear reflection of his professional -- by the contents of the books is a reflection of his own activities and knowledge of 1991, together with the statements Kadijevic made during that period -- time period, and there is for example in my report a statement which is from the 3rd of October, 65 ter number 506, which is quoted on page 16 in the English version. These are official points of view of a senior official who was extremely well-placed to have such views. So in the official statements, I think that they have quite some weight, when one has to analyse the events of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, but will you agree with me that Mr. Kadijevic wrote the book at a time when he was no longer defence minister or federal secretary for All People's Defence? The statement that you have just referred to does not say that the objectives of the armed forces of the SFRY were ever changed in relation to what was envisioned in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It is correct, Your Honours, that the book dates from 1993, but I would assume that, judging by the contents of the book, that Kadijevic had an authorisation to publish all -- or to publish it, including the contents, and in relation to the statement, but it's obvious that it's not openly mentioned that -- the goals I've mentioned that have changed, but when I look at how the mission of the armed forces is defined in this statement from the 3rd of October, and when I compare it to the constitutional mission, one has the impression, the strong impression there has been a change in the mission of the SFRY armed forces. And I can also add that the statement by General Adzic, who was then the chief of General Staff, 12th of October, 1991, which has been exhibited as Exhibit 89, which is mentioned on page 17 to page 19 on my report. Second part.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Theunens, but Mr. Kadijevic's statement of the 3rd of October does not say anything about any such changes. It is your opinion that changes occurred, in relation to the objectives of the army under the powers granted the arm by the constitution, but this isn't something that Mr. Kadijevic actually stated, is it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can read out a paragraph that is relevant in the context of the question of Mr. Vasic. It's on the bottom of English page 16. "The army now wants nothing more but to restore control in the crisis areas to protect the Serbian population from persecution and annihilations and to liberate the army personnel and members of their families, the conditions for this is to defeat Ustashi forces." Now, it is obvious that the wording is -- is like -- it's much shorter and it's only one statement I have quoted now from there, other official statements, included my report, but when you compare this here with the constitutional mission, I think one would conclude that there are some differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I understand that you have a need to explain and to answer the question, but I asked you very specifically about the statement of the 3rd of October, whereas you gave us a reply now confirming that this is your opinion that the objectives had been changed. It's not contained in the statement. I would like to know whether you came across a fact stemming from this statement that you just read out. What is it that threatened the Serb residents in the territory of Croatia? Are you aware of this? Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, there are at least two or three questions in your state -- in your question now. What I read out comes from the statement from Kadijevic on the 3rd of October. Now, based on what he writes, the Serbian population needed to be protected from -- by the JNA from persecution and annihilation, and the army personnel and members of their families had to be liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: They should have been protected from whom, these Serbs? And also, who imprisoned the officers and their families? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Based on Kadijevic's statement, as well as Adzic's -- so General Adzic's statement, which is -- actually follows Kadijevic's statement in my report, Adzic -- excuse me, in the letter 6-83, speaks about the requirement to defend parts of the Serbian people from genocide and biological extermination at the hands of Ustasha forces. Now, it is not part of my report to analyse what happened or did not happen with Serbs in Croatia. This information -- information in this section here, section 1 of the second part, is intended to explain whether or not there was a change in the mission of the JNA during the armed conflict in Croatia. And I leave it up to the reader to draw his or her conclusions. I can only quote from sources, and indeed have the reader then conclude what he or she thinks happened or didn't happened with the mission -- to the mission of the JNA and the SFRY armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, can we agree that you believe that your assessment of the evolution of the tasks and the role of the JNA in the armed conflict in Croatia, that you reached that assessment by analysing the conduct of only one party to the conflict. However, a conflict is unavoidably an interaction between two parties to a conflict.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It is indeed correct, Your Honours, that a conflict involves two or even more parties, but I believe that the information provided by Generals Kadijevic and Adzic, because of their senior position and their role at the time of the events, is very useful to understand the mission of the JNA and what remained of the SFRY armed forces during the time period that is of interest for us, i.e. the latter half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. You are right, I should have said that an armed conflict is an interaction of at least two warring parties. Now let us turn to page 6 in B/C/S, in English it's page 5. And then under paragraph 8 you speak of documents that are kept in some units, and then you also mention a war log or a war diary that is normally kept for the duration of the war. Tell me, please, in addition to this war log, was there also an operations diary in the JNA units, and in addition to that, was there also a book of reporting? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I am familiar with that, Your Honours, but I'm not sure about the reference -- I mean I speak in my report in section 1 about a war diary, and that's on page 60, which is an -- which comes from -- for example, in the 1988 JNA battalion manual, which is Exhibit 397, a war log-book is mentioned. I am familiar with the fact that units can also have an operational diary. The OTP has requested the operations diary of the Guards Motorised Brigade, and that's already some time ago, but we haven't requested [sic] It yet, so ... And, I'm sorry, the book of reporting I'm -- I learned through a witness interview that such a book exists. There is a actually a kind of register of incoming and outgoing orders, which we have requested from Serbia and Montenegro, I mean the one for the Guards Motorised Brigade covering time period the Guards Motorised Brigade was involved in the operations in Vukovar. It was obtained after the filing of this report, so it was not included in the report, it was disclosed to the Defence. We also requested an -- a register of orders and reports that have been received by telephone, and so far we have no answer to that request.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You gave me an answer to the question that I was about to put to you. Tell me, please, is there a book of reporting, a book where all reports of subordinate units are compiled, those given at daily briefings, and all orders that are then issued by commanders based on those reports, and this is all done during regular daily briefings?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm -- I'm not familiar with -- with such a book. In relation to the regular daily briefings, we have requested, actually, the minutes, I'm just trying to -- whether I can find it here on the spot. Yes, request 892 from -- I apologise. From the 5th of August, 2005, we requested from Serbia and Montenegro the minutes and lists of participants of the daily command meetings that took place at the headquarters of OG South (Guards Motorised Brigade) in Negoslavci, between 30 September and 23rd of November, 1991. We received a reply on the 15th of November, 2005 from the competent authorities in Serbia and Montenegro at the time stating, "There are no minutes of the daily command briefings at the command post or headquarters of OG South." On the 30th of November, 2005, we received a similar reply, confirming, basically, the reply of the 15th of November. So that's all I can answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic. We must adjourn now for the day, resuming at 9.30 in the morning. And I think, Mr. Vasic, you have 50 minutes remaining. Five zero minutes remaining.
